title: Ultrahigh-Sensitivity Mass Spectrometry for Scalable Proteomics
text:
Research on aging is currently hindered by a lack of high-sensitivity technologies capable of characterizing
proteins in limited cell populations and biopsies. This proposal will develop a next-generation ultrahigh-
sensitive instrument to enable the deep analysis of proteins in important biological models of aging.

title: Molecular mechanisms for regulating microRNA levels in metazoans
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNA) are small RNA molecules that are important for controlling animal developmental,
differentiation, and disease processes. We are investigating how the cellular levels of miRNAs are precisely
controlled through regulation of their biogenesis and degradation. This research will reveal the pathological
consequences related to dysregulated miRNA levels in disease and provide the basis for designing therapeutic
molecular tools to control gene expression via miRNAs.

title: Functional Genomics of Treponema pallidum during Human Infection
text:
PROJECT RELEVANCE NARRATIVE
 This project supports the NIH mission by advancing our understanding of Treponema pallidum
pathogenesis, which is crucial for combating syphilis. By analyzing the bacterium’s gene expression profile from
human syphilis clinical samples, we aim to uncover new avenues for diagnostics, treatments, and vaccines. This
endeavor supports the NIH’s goal of fostering groundbreaking medical research to reduce the disease burden
of syphilis and enhance human health.

title: Duke Immune Profiling Core
text: The Duke Immune Profiling Core (DIPC) is a Duke Cancer Institute – CCSG designated Shared Resource. The overarching goal of the DIPC is to impact cancer diagnosis and treatment by providing DCI investigators with highest quality human immune profiling data in support of their innovative clinical studies. The DIPC shared resource is comprised of 2 components. The first is a Service component in which DIPC provides comprehensive, highly standardized, state-of-the-art human immunologic profiling services in support of both intra- and extra-mural translational research endeavors, including Phase I/II clinical trials. The second DIPC component focuses on Discovery and utilizes advanced, high-dimensional immunobiologic technologies and resources to stimulate innovative translational research initiatives that will impact existing approaches to cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. With over 60 years of experience in flow cytometry and immune profiling, we are available to support a wide range of studies from small-scale projects for generating pilot data through clinical trial testing. Additionally, our services include study design, performance of experiments, data collection and analysis, and writing support. Moving forward, we will further enhance our data acquisition and analytical capacity in order to provide DCI members with innovative methods to evaluate patient specimens. The DIPC Shared Resource, which has been in existence since 2019, has provided services to 83 DCI investigators, accounting for 54% of total usage, from all 7 DCI Research Programs during this grant period. During the same period, DIPC provided immune profiling support for 5 cancer immunotherapy clinical trials, and anticipates supporting up to 10 such trials during the next 5-year funding period. Use of this Shared Resource by DCI members contributed to 12 publications over the current project period, 6 of which appeared in high impact journals.

title: BCM/TSU P20  Collaborative Cancer Research Education Program (C-REP)
text:
CURED C-REP Project Narrative 
The CURED C-REP will provide an 8-weeks mentored cancer research experience that integrates Baylor College of Medicine (BCM) and Texas Southern University (TSU) infrastructures every summer followed by year- long outreach education activities that will increase the awareness, knowledge, and understanding of research, concepts, processes, and careers in cancer research/cancer health outcomes in a cohort of 20 TSU students. The proposed CURED C-REP will enhance cancer research education capacity at TSU, enhance workforce development, and improve BCM’s effectiveness in developing and sustaining research programs focused on cancer health outcomes.

title: Defining the role of G3BP1 in vascular development
text:
Proper blood vessel formation in embryos is crucial for lifelong cardiovascular health. Understanding the
molecular mechanisms behind this process, including the role of RNA binding protein G3BP1, is vital. G3BP1's
regulation of blood vessel formation offers potential therapeutic targets for correcting issues in cardiovascular
disease and cancer.

title: Biophysical mechanisms for bidirectional coupling between mechanotransduction and cell morphology
text:
Cells in human tissues must respond to a variety of biochemical and physical cues from the surrounding
extracellular space. This project integrates biophysical experiments measuring cell response to nanoscale
curvature and biochemical stimuli with detailed spatiotemporal computational models of cellular signaling and
deformation. By using experiments to inform and parameterize models, this work promises to enable predictive
simulations of cellular responses to microenvironmental changes in healthy and diseased conditions.

title: Defining the roles of FHR1 in complement-mediated glomerular endothelial injury
text:
Complement provides a rapid and effective immune response but requires precise regulation
to prevent excessive activation and healthy tissue injury. Factor H and Factor H Related (FHR) proteins work
together to achieve this balance, and when FHR1 is mutated, it causes severe complement dysregulation and
life-threatening kidney disease, particularly through damage to the small vessels of the kidney. This research
uses biochemical, cellular, and animal models to better understand how FHR1 affects kidney blood vessels in
complement-associated injuries, informing our understanding of kidney disease and identifying novel treatment
targets.

title: Network-based Framework to Decode Novel Gain-of-Function Mutations and their Mechanistic Roles in General Human Diseases
text:
The identification of genetic variants that impact function and phenotype is fundamental to our
understanding of the molecular mechanisms of disease and the practice of precision medicine. Research
in my laboratory is focused on developing and implementing computational and bioinformatic
technologies to understand the functional effects of genetic mutations on molecular interaction networks
and gene regulatory networks, bridging genotype and phenotype in health and disease. In the next five
years, by developing a set of innovative deep learning and language models, we will accurately predict
and validate the functional effects of genetic mutations on protein-protein interactions, gene-environment
interactions, and genetic interactions, and we envision that our efforts will be instrumental to push current
human genetics research paradigm towards a thorough functional and quantitative modeling of all
genomic mutations involved in disease development and progression.

title: Primary Cilia-Dependent Mechanisms of Lymphangiogenesis
text: Properly patterned lymphatic vessels are critical regulators of fluid and cellular traffic to support an effective inflammation and wound healing response. However, the mechanisms that govern lymphatic vessel patterning are not fully understood, and new therapeutics are needed to treat dysregulations of lymphangiogenesis, for example in neovascularized corneal transplant rejection, lymphedema, and tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis. The long-term goal of this research program is to develop lymphatic-targeted strategies to promote wound healing and prevent or reverse refractory inflammation. In the course of work examining lymphatic vessel pathology, the current investigators recently identified primary cilia on lymphatic endothelial cells in vitro and in vivo. In other cell types, this organelle is a hub of cell signaling and regulates cellular processes such as proliferation, cell polarity, and migration. Preliminary data in knockout mouse models of IFT20, an intraflagellar transport protein important for primary cilia function, show that loss of primary cilia exacerbates lymphangiogenesis. This suggests that previously unappreciated primary cilia-dependent mechanisms may complement and modulate canonical mechanisms of lymphangiogenesis regulation. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that unknown primary cilia signaling pathways negatively regulate excessive lymphangiogenesis by suppressing sprouting, proliferation, and migration to form vasculature appropriately tuned to local demand. This hypothesis will be tested with two specific aims: (1) Identify the cellular mechanisms by which loss of primary cilia dysregulates lymphangiogenesis; and (2) Identify lymphatic endothelial cell signaling pathways that are disrupted by loss of primary cilia. In aim 1, intravital imaging in mice with IFT20 knockout and tdTomato reporter fluorescence along with in vitro lymphangiogenesis assays will be used to identify the timing and extent of dysregulation of specific lymphatic endothelial cell activities that comprise a functional lymphangiogenesis response, such as sprouting, cell-cell junction organization, and chemotaxis. In aim 2, two next generation sequencing technologies, RNA-Seq and spatial transcriptomics, will be used in combination with pathway analysis and gene ontology strategies and rational hypothesis-driven prioritization of hits to identify candidate primary cilia-dependent regulators of inflammation-associated corneal lymphangiogenesis. Candidates will be validated in vitro in CRISPR knockout lymphatic endothelial cell lines. The combination of intravital imaging, transcriptomics, gene editing, and a panel of in vitro lymphangiogenesis assays is an innovative strategy to comprehensively interrogate the cellular mechanistic basis of primary cilia regulation of lymphangiogenesis. The proposed project is significant because it will provide the first mechanistic insight into primary cilia function in lymphatic endothelial cells with the potential to provide novel therapeutic targets to control lymphangiogenesis as well as a framework for study of primary cilia regulation of other lymphatic remodeling events. This work may open a new frontier for the field of lymphatic vessel biology.

title: Advancing TGFβ-Resistant CAR-NK Cell Therapy for Acute Myeloid Leukemia
text:
In this proposal, we seek to improve treatment outcomes for patients with relapsed/refractory AML
by evaluating the safety and efficacy of cord blood derived TGFBR2 KO iC9/CAR27-28ζ/IL-15 NK
cells in a Phase I/II trial. Moreover, leveraging our robust genome-wide CRISPR screening
platform we aim to uncover novel mechanisms of resistance to design next-generation CAR-NK
cells that can improve outcomes of patients with AML.

title: Sex differences in cholinergic signaling in alcohol withdrawal
text:
The goal of this project is to investigate sex differences in cholinergic mechanisms that mediate negative affect
and behavioral symptoms of prolonged alcohol withdrawal in male and female mice. By defining the key players
and sites of action, this proposal will contribute to fundamental knowledge about sex differences in alcohol
withdrawal, provide a rigorous basis for subsequent research and unveil potential targets for
pharmacotherapeutic intervention that can be tailored by sex.

title: Tau-mediated synaptic dysfunction in age-related neurodegenerative diseases
text:
As the human population ages, the ability to maintain cognitive function with a brain accumulating tau pathology
relies on the preservation and maintenance of synaptic networks. Therefore, understanding the mechanism by
which tau contributes to network and synapse dysfunction is critical for developing preventative therapeutics.
This proposal aims to determine the cellular mechanisms(s) by which pathologic tau drives neuronal network
dysfunction and propose a training plan catered to the applicant that will promote success as an independent
researcher in the field of aging research.

title: Non-viral gene delivery platforms for the treatment of Usher Syndrome Type 2A.
text:
Mutations in USH2A, which are responsible for ~85% of all USH2 cases, lead to severe auditory defects and
late onset retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and in some cases autosomal recessive non-syndromic RP. Developing
an effective treatment for USH2A has been challenging due to its very large coding sequence and the presence
of isoforms with functions that are not fully understood. We aim to extend the benefits of our proven non-viral
gene therapy platform consisting of nanoparticles, nanospheres, and sulfotyrosine to enhance delivery,
protection, controlled release, and distribution of intravitreally delivered Ush2a gene to rescue vision loss
associated with USH2A.

title: A synaptic substrate for ketamine-mediated amelioration of stress-induced anhedonia
text:
There is a major unmet need for the treatment of depression because current pharmacotherapies for depression
require prolonged administration for clinical improvement and they are often associated with high non-response
rate. Recent clinical evidence has shown that a single sub-anesthetic dose of ketamine, a glutamate-NMDA
receptor antagonist, induces a robust antidepressant effect within hours of treatment in 70% of treatment-
resistant patients, however a circuit and synaptic-level dissection of ketamine’s mechanisms of action is
lacking. Accordingly, the goal of this proposal is to identify circuits, cellular and molecular determinants
responsible for the rapid antidepressant action of ketamine.

title: Genetics of Cardiometabolic Diseases in the VA Population
text:
Cardiometabolic disorders including obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and type 2 diabetes
are highly prevalent among U.S. Veterans and serve as major factors in the development of heart,
vascular and liver diseases. We have assembled a multi-disciplinary research team comprised
of investigators with expertise in cardiovascular and metabolic disease, clinical and
epidemiological research, EHR based research methods, genetic epidemiology, and statistical
genetics. We now propose to build upon the momentum of our currently funded project (“Genetics
of Cardiometabolic Diseases in the VA Population”) and further elucidate the genetic basis of the
longitudinal progression of cardiometabolic traits, thereby informing more targeted genomic
medicine-based disease management throughout the course of Veterans' lives.

title: Vision Bioinformatics and Computation
text:
VISION BIOINFORMATICS and COMPUTATION MODULE
Project Narrative
The goal of the Vision Bioinformatics & Computation (VBC) module is to increase our
understanding of biological processes in vision research by applying state-of-art techniques
specifically bioinformatics and custom programming. Through VBC, NEI R01 investigators will
have easy access to high-level expertise in vision bioinformatics and custom programming as well
as the support needed to design, execute, analyze, interpret, and manage results required or
facilitated by informatics and computational applications. VBC offers expertise to develop novel
tools, software, and analytical pipelines for the integration, annotation, analysis, retrieval, and
presentation of these data from basic and clinical studies of eye diseases.

title: Targeting EBV's Deubiquitinating Activity for Therapy
text:
This proposal focuses on the Epstein-Barr Virus deubiquitinating enzyme, BPLF1, that removes the ubiquitin
modifier from protein targets and thus affects their function. This proposed research aims to identify an inhibitor
of BPLF1 which could serve as therapy for EBV associated diseases.

title: Piezo1- Mediated Type H Vessel Formation in Periodontitis
text:
This study is proposed to determine the role of recently identified subset of endothelial cells, i.e., type H vessel,
in the induction and maintenance of osteogenesis in the alveolar bone affected by periodontitis. Since bone
regeneration in the alveolar bone defect caused by periodontitis has been major challenge in the periodontitis
research and none of the study has ever addressed the coupling between angiogenesis and osteogenesis, this
study is anticipated to cause a paradigm shift in the field. Outcomes from this project will be translated into a
novel therapeutic approach not only to prevent pathogenic bone resorption, but also to induce bone regeneration
in periodontitis.

title: Multi-omic dissection of clonal hematopoiesis-associated diseases
text:
Somatic mutations accumulated with aging and/or in response to environmental insult and chronic
inflammation can confer a selective advantage leading to clonal expansion in hematopoietic stem cells, a
phenomenon termed 'Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential' (CHIP). CHIP has been associated with
a selective range of non-hematopoietic conditions, including coronary artery disease, stroke, heart failure,
venous thromboembolism, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic liver diseases, and osteoporosis,
yet the molecular mechanisms by which CHIP specifically promotes these diseases remain largely unknown. I
will leverage large-scale multi-omics data to molecularly connect CHIP with the development of associated
diseases and identify the mechanisms underlying CHIP-associated disease risks and thus prioritize therapeutic
targets.
